Jasper and Finny stood at the edge of Miller’s Gulch, peering through the tangled briar into the shadow of the old grist mill. The structure loomed like a hunched, gray creature, its windows like vacant eyes, its timbers groaning softly in the breeze. Pip, smaller and paler than his companions, clutched his worn cap.

“Now, ain’t she a beauty!” said Jasper, puffing out his chest and trying to make his voice sound deep. “Best haunted house in five counties, I reckon.”

“You think there’s really ghosts in there, Jas?” Finny whispered, though he squinted his eyes to appear brave. “Old Man Hemlock swore he saw a blue light in the topmost window, just last Tuesday week.”

“Blue light, shmoolight,” Jasper scoffed, though a shiver ran down his own spine. “’Course there’s ghosts. And treasures, too, I bet. Old Man Miller was rich as mud, they say, before he went plumb crazy and boarded the place up. Left all his gold and jewels just sitting there, waiting for someone with enough grit to go fetch ’em.”

“But what if the ghosts get us?” Pip whimpered, his eyes wide.

“Ghosts don’t get nobody who ain’t got a yellow streak down their back, Pip,” Jasper declared, turning to him with a stern look. “And we ain’t got no yellow streaks, me and Finny, do we, Finny?”

“Not a one,” Finny echoed, trying to sound as resolute as Jasper, but his voice cracked a little at the end. “We’re tough as old shoe leather, us.”

“That’s right. Now, here’s the plan. We go in through that broken cellar door, see? Then we search the main floor, look for the big iron safe folks used to talk about. And Pip, you stand guard by the door. You holler if you hear anything, mind.”

“Me?” Pip’s voice was barely audible. “But what if something comes out?”

“Then you holler louder, silly,” Jasper grinned, nudging Finny. “You think we’re scared, Pip? Why, many a time I’ve looked at this old mill, and thought, well, I wish I could go in; but I never thought I could until now.”

“Me neither,” said Finny. “I always figured it was too dangerous. But with you, Jas, it’s just nothing.”

“That’s the spirit,” Jasper said, and he began to push aside the heavy briars. “Don’t you worry, Pip. We’ll be in and out quicker than a fly in a buttermilk churn. And we’ll have more stories to tell than old Aunt Martha has wrinkles.”

They edged their way through the scratchy tangle of thorns and rusted wire, Pip lagging a little behind, his heart thumping like a trapped bird. The air grew damp and heavy as they approached the broken cellar door, and a strange, musty smell, like forgotten leaves and damp earth, wafted out. Jasper pushed at the splintered wood, and it groaned open with a sound like an old man sighing. A deeper darkness lay beyond, cool and still.

“Alright, Finny, you go first,” Jasper commanded, stepping back slightly.

Finny gulped. “Me? But Jas, you’re the leader. Leaders always go first.”

“Leaders make the plans, Finny. Foot soldiers execute ‘em,” Jasper retorted, pushing him gently forward. Finny stumbled into the darkness, and Jasper followed, Pip peering anxiously from the entrance. The light from outside dimmed, swallowed by the mill’s deep maw; they could hear the drip-drip of water somewhere in the gloom, and the rustle of unseen creatures.

“See? Nothing to it,” Jasper said, his voice a little hoarse, though he tried to sound confident. “Just a bit of old dust and cobwebs.”

Suddenly, a distinct scraping sound echoed from deeper within the mill, a sort of dragging, shuffling noise, followed by a faint, metallic clinking. All three boys froze. Pip, outside, let out a small, choked gasp. Jasper and Finny pressed themselves against the damp stone wall, their eyes wide and straining. The sounds grew louder, closer, like something heavy being moved by an unseen hand. A chill, colder than the cellar air, crept up their spines.

“What was that!” Finny whispered, his voice trembling like a leaf.

“Just… just the wind, probably,” Jasper stammered, though there was no wind stirring in the stagnant air of the mill.

Then, a low, drawn-out moan drifted from the darkness, a sound so desolate and sorrowful it made the very hairs on their necks stand on end. It was not the sighing of the wind, nor the groan of old timbers. It was a sound of true, unbearable misery. Both boys’ faces turned a ghastly white; every nerve in their bodies screamed for escape.

A large, dark shape detached itself from the deeper shadows, slowly moving towards them. It seemed to sway, and from it emanated another, deeper moan, followed by a clatter. Finny let out a strangled cry, and without a word, turned and bolted. Jasper, seeing his comrade’s sudden flight, didn’t hesitate. He scrambled out of the cellar opening, tripping over Pip, who was already turning to flee.

They ran as they had never run before, crashing through the briars, heedless of the scratches and tears in their clothes. They didn’t stop until they were well clear of Miller’s Gulch, breathless and panting, their hearts still hammering against their ribs. Finny was sobbing quietly, his face buried in his hands. Pip was curled into a ball, whimpering. Jasper, though his own legs felt like water and his throat was tight with suppressed fear, tried to regain some semblance of composure.

“Well,” he puffed, wiping a tear from his eye that he hoped Finny hadn’t seen, “that was… an adventure, wasn’t it?”

Finny sniffled, looking up. “Jas, I think… I think it was a ghost. A real, live ghost.”

“Nonsense,” Jasper said, though his voice was still shaky. “Probably just… just a stray dog, or some old raccoons, making a ruckus in there. Sound travels funny, you know. Or maybe… maybe it was just a rat, a big rat.” He tried to sound convincing, but even to his own ears, it rang hollow.

“It moaned, Jas!” Pip wailed. “Dogs don’t moan like that; and rats don’t clank!”

Jasper cleared his throat, trying to summon a look of unconcern. “Well, whatever it was, we certainly showed it a thing or two, didn’t we? Ran right out of there before it knew what hit it. Good thing we were so fast.”

“Yeah, real fast,” Finny muttered, rubbing his scraped knee.

“Now, listen here, boys,” Jasper said, lowering his voice conspiratorially. “We don’t tell nobody about… about the moaning part, understand? We tell ‘em we explored the whole mill, top to bottom, saw the old safe, even heard something, but we scared it off, right? And we didn’t find any treasure, ’cause the ghosts had already moved it, see?”

Finny and Pip exchanged a glance. Finny nodded slowly. “Yeah. Yeah, that’s a good story. We were real brave.”

“Brave as lions,” Jasper agreed, a faint blush returning to his cheeks. “Just… just don’t go back in there anytime soon, alright? It’s not polite to disturb old ghosts, not after we’ve had our fun with ‘em.”

They walked home in a subdued silence, the afternoon sun feeling surprisingly bright and warm on their pale faces. That night, at supper, Jasper and Finny ate little. When their mothers asked why they were so quiet, they mumbled something about not feeling well, perhaps too much pie at old Mrs. Higgins’s earlier. Pip, however, kept glancing nervously towards the window, half expecting a blue light to appear in the distance, and he didn’t eat a bite. And for many a week after, the path to Miller’s Gulch remained remarkably undisturbed, the old mill left to its creaking timbers and its silent, dusty secrets.
